### PARENT NATIONAL FRAMEWORK (shared context for every dossier — no score is given)

ASSESSMENT
The country offers no route to legal gender recognition. A law signed by the president in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents. A trans visitor's passport, visa and identity papers therefore remain as issued, and no procedure exists in the country to align them with the holder's gender. The national supreme court designated the non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist in November 2023. An international human rights organisation counted 101 extremism-related convictions by June 2025 for alleged participation in the movement or display of its symbols, with charges brought under both administrative and criminal codes. Arrests have followed for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Between March and May 2026 nine organisations were outlawed as extremist. The propaganda statutes reach expression. The 2013 law covered material concerning minors; a December 2022 amendment extended it to all age groups, and it now prohibits material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships and material that gives minors a "desire to change their sex". More than 180 enforcement cases were opened in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined, with fines of about 26 million rubles. A news outlet reported in June 2025 that propaganda cases had grown eighteenfold over the previous decade and that fines under the statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in two years. Enforcement has reached venues. Within 48 hours of the November 2023 designation, masked police raided LGBT-friendly bars in the capital; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face the walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. A news outlet reported in June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBT life in the country through the year. Detention carries lethal risk. In December 2024 a man arrested on extremism-related charges over an LGBT travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. The law provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and motivation by sexual orientation or gender identity is not an aggravating factor in sentencing. The government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBT community. Partner recognition is unavailable. Neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions exist, and a 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage. A regional human rights court held in 2021 that the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships violated the convention; the country left the court in 2022. The 2023 gender-transition law deems a marriage void where a trans person marries someone of their same birth sex, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognised status. One national government maintains its highest-level "do not travel" advisory for the country, with warnings relevant to LGBT travellers. Public attitudes are hostile. A 2022 survey found 74% of respondents said homosexuality should not be accepted by society, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey showed support for equal rights for gays and lesbians had fallen to 33%.

SECONDARY / SITUATIONAL FACTORS
A national government's country policy note, issued in 2025 and updated in 2026, treats LGBT+ people in the country, including one region, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for that country's asylum claims. Emigration has become a route out. A publication reported in August 2024 that the extremism designation drove a purge and mass emigration of LGBT people, and a news outlet reported in June 2024 that emigration had become the only means of survival for many trans people, profiling those caught between leaving and staying. A news agency reported in December 2024 that the LGBT community was living in fear after the new laws and court rulings, pushed into silence, flight and self-censorship. The international human rights organisation called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing.

AFFECTS RESIDENTS MORE THAN VISITORS
The 2023 law deprives people diagnosed with gender dysphoria of the right to adopt children. A 2024 law bans adoption of children in the country by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions. A news service reported in July 2024 on a trans woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre in a remote region. She was held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour, and escaped when police responded to a phone she found. The capital's authorities have never approved a request to hold a pride rally, and in 2010 a regional human rights court fined the country for systematically refusing pride parade permits. A queer woman in a second city described waking up to find herself "a second-class citizen" after the national supreme court's extremist designation.

SOURCE EVIDENCE (first 8)
- An official country-policy assessment (June 2025; page updated later): LGBT+ people in the nation — including one region — constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for asylum claims elsewhere; external-protection framework, dated 2025-26.
- A travel-advisory page could not be retrieved at research time (access error); the underlying advisory (highest 'do not travel' level) includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.
- A monitoring organisation (June 2025): courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for alleged participation in a designated movement or displaying its alleged symbols; the charges span administrative and criminal codes, and the organisation calls on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the nation.
- Independent reporting (June 2025): after a 2023 designation of a non-existent 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, cases under the nation's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought over 60 million rubles into the national budget in the past two years.
- Reporting (June 2025): arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025 — a queer woman describes waking up to find herself 'a second-class citizen' after the designation.
- Reporting (Dec 2024): 'a man arrested for allegedly running an LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in custody' — detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business, found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
- Reporting (Dec 2024): the nation's LGBTQ+ community is living in fear following new laws and court rulings, activists say — the post-designation crackdown pushes people into silence, flight and self-censorship.
- An international-affairs magazine (Aug 2024): how the extremism designation fuelled a purge and mass emigration of LGBT citizens.

### DIVISION LOCAL EVIDENCE
Under occupation by a neighbouring state since 2014, the peninsula is governed by the occupying state's full legal regime: a "propaganda" law extended to all audiences, a 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming medical care, and a supreme-court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, with participation or financing punishable by up to twelve years in prison. Local courts fine people tens of thousands of currency units for "propaganda" — books, images and social-media posts — with penalties exceeding the average local wage. The occupation leadership has openly threatened LGBT people, promising that "self-defense forces and police will react" to any gay street presence; a militia threatened to "pack and post" LGBT people out of the peninsula. No public LGBT event has taken place since the occupation began. International monitors are barred from entering. An interview-based human-rights report documents a foreigner lured via a fake dating profile into an apartment where five men stripped and beat him, forced him to lick a toilet, filmed the assault and published the video — a documented visitor-facing predation pattern with no police recourse. A 2025 assessment reports violent attacks on LGBT people and those perceived as LGBT, almost all openly LGBT residents having fled, and those remaining not expressing identity visibly. The occupying state's legal gender-change procedures were unusable in practice under the occupation authorities even when nominally available
